**What changes**
- Under current rules, replacement candidates are chosen in the same election as the recall question.
- If it passes, vacancies would instead be addressed through a later special election or an appointment.

**Replacement rules by office (CalMatters explainer, calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-5-explainer/)**
- Within roughly four months, a special election would fill a recalled legislator's seat, and the lawmaker who was recalled could seek it again.
- For statewide posts such as treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner, a gubernatorial appointee would fill the vacancy until the next regular election.
- Per the CaVotes summary, recalls in a term's first two years would push the replacement decision to the next statewide vote, with the winner finishing out the term. The two summaries describe timing differently, so check the measure text for specifics.

**Arguments**
- Backers, including the League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause, say the change would stop replacement winners from taking office with a small share of the vote. The California GOP and the Election Integrity Project also warn that letting the lieutenant governor take over a recalled governor's job could discourage recall turnout.
- Fiscal effects could run into the millions in either direction, depending on which office is recalled, and costs could climb if a follow-up special election is needed.

**CalMatters coverage**
- The explainer casts the measure as a Democratic-driven push to rewrite recall rules, with voters holding the final word.
- One account traces the measure to Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Newman, while KPBS's copy of the same explainer links it to a Secretary of State proposal that followed the 2021 recall.
- The ballot title, "Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers," could mislead voters, since lawmakers aren't statewide officials even though every legislative race would be touched.

A constitutional amendment the Legislature referred to voters.

**What it does**
- Removes the replacement question from recall ballots, so voters decide only on removal. "Voters would decide only whether to remove the official."
- A simple majority of yes votes removes the official. The seat then goes to an appointee or a special election, based on which office it is.

**Vacancy rules by office and timing**
- **Governor recalled:**
  - Within the first 24 months: the lieutenant governor serves in the interim, and a replacement vote in the next statewide contest picks who finishes the term.
  - Later: the lieutenant governor finishes the term instead.
- **Other statewide offices** (examples: lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state): the governor names a replacement to finish out the term.
- **Legislative seats:** usually filled through a special election.

"The recalled official may not be appointed to the same office but could run in a special election." Under current rules, a recalled official cannot be a replacement candidate, so this would be a change. The page doesn't say whether this also covers a governor's replacement vote.

- Statewide recalls would involve officials in all 58 counties. District recalls would involve only officials in that district.
- Dropping the replacement question might trim spending, while a later special vote could add expense.

- Prop. 5 would drop what the article calls "the second question": who replaces an official who is recalled.
- The article describes the new system this way: "Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election."
- Under current rules, the top vote-getter wins the replacement race, even without a majority.
- Legislative races would also be affected, even though the ballot title mentions only statewide officers.

**Vacancies and special-election timing, by office**
- **Governor:** If recalled in the first two years, the secretary of state calls a special election (the article gives no timeline). If recalled in the final two years, the lieutenant governor completes the term.
- **Lieutenant governor:** The article doesn't say how this vacancy would be filled.
- **Other statewide officers** (e.g., treasurer, attorney general, insurance commissioner): The governor appoints a replacement who serves until the next regular election. No special election is described.
- **Legislators** (state senators and Assembly members): The governor must issue the call within roughly four months, setting up a special election.
- **Other local offices:** The article doesn't address these.

**Can the recalled official run?**
- Per the article: "The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election." It doesn't say whether this applies to statewide officials, who would be replaced by appointment instead.

**Supporters and their reasons**
- **Who:** Democratic lawmakers who placed it on the ballot in 2024, the secretary of state, and the good-governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters.
- **Why:** It responds to the 2021 attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom, which failed. She sees that drop as a likely "guiding force" behind Democrats' support, since they win more races.
- **Author Josh Newman** calls that kind of targeting "political gamesmanship," which he says isn't what Gov. Hiram Johnson had in mind for the 1911 recall law. He says he did nothing more than "cast a tough vote."

He also says added special votes would drive up taxpayer costs.

- The article cites no official fiscal analysis. Its only cost figure comes from DeMaio's argument: the attempted 2021 recall of Newsom "cost about $200 million to administer," and that cost "would double if there were two separate elections."

- A PPIC poll from early September found: "59% of likely voters said they likely would vote 'no' and just 35% said they would vote 'yes.'"

**Endorsement:** Yes. The board "strongly urges a 'yes' vote on Proposition 5."

**Publication:** McClatchy Media's California editorial board, speaking for The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee, and San Luis Obispo Tribune. Dated Sept. 18, 2026, and appears on Yahoo News.

**Core reasoning:** Under the current two-question system, replacements can win without majority support, while Prop. 5 would better respect majority rule. The board also notes that recalls are rare, with 11 state efforts reaching the ballot since 1913.

**What Prop. 5 would change** (for legislators and statewide constitutional officers)
- **Ballot:** Today, a qualifying recall asks whether to remove the official and who would take over. "If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated."
- **Legislative seats:** A recalled legislator's seat would stay open pending a special election.
- **Constitutional officers:** The governor would fill the vacancy.
- **Governors:** A recall during the initial two years would have the lieutenant governor take over the governorship in the interim, pending a special election. Later recalls would keep the lieutenant governor in place until the next regular election.
- **Can a recalled official run?** Yes, according to the article. Prop. 5 would "allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy."

**Benefits the board names**
- **Deliberate, majority-based process:** The board admits the process would be slower, calling it "a longer process, but also one that's more thoughtful, deliberate," and says it better honors majority rule.
- **Minority winners:** Since 1911, five replacements have won with under half the vote. Because the top vote-getter wins, a recalled official can outpoll the replacement: "a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate."
- **2018 example:** Ling Ling Chang won with just under 34%, while nearly 42% opposed recalling Josh Newman. Newman, who later regained his seat and went on to author Prop. 5, said: "So I got more votes by way of 'no, don't kick him out,'"
- **Critics of the current system:** Some view it as "a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don't like," a view the board attributes to the League of Women Voters and similar groups.
- **Acknowledged limits:** The board concedes Prop. 5 won't end "political gamesmanship," but says it can "safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule."

**Concerns raised by opponents, and the board's responses**
- **Dodging recalls:** Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, an outspoken opponent who backed Newman's 2017 recall, sees the measure as the ruling party trying to dodge recalls. He warns officials could say: "Don't vote for the recall or else you won't be represented for 12 months." The board counters by citing the state constitution's timing rules: a recall election within 60 to 80 days after certification, or up to 180 days if combined with a regular election.
- **Special-election costs and recalled officials:** Opponents decry the expense of special elections and object to letting ousted officials run in one. The board doesn't directly answer either point, though it concedes the process would take longer.
- **Broader rebuttal:** The board says opponents overlook how replacements have already won without majority support under today's rules.

I can't reproduce the full analysis verbatim, so this condenses each section and quotes the key sentences.

**Summary**
- **In short:** Proposition 5 would drop the replacement question from recall ballots and change how vacancies get filled.
- **Yes vote:** "Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy." Vacancies would generally be filled by special election or appointment instead.
- **No vote:** "Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections."
- **Fiscal bottom line:** "Net fiscal effect unknown." The possible costs or savings, which the analysis says "would be rare," could reach millions per recall, depending on which office is recalled and how frequently recalls happen.

**Background**
- **Terms and elections:** Assembly members serve two-year terms and governors serve four-year terms. Regular statewide votes come every two years, and special elections can be called in addition.
- **Recalls:** Supporters need a fixed count of signatures from the affected district, or from across the state for statewide posts. Since 1913, eleven state recall efforts have reached the ballot, and six led to removal.
- **Two-question ballot:** Voters answer whether to remove the official and who would replace them if removed. The top vote-getter on the second question takes office. The 2003 governor recall listed 135 replacement candidates; the 2021 one listed 46.
- **Vacancies outside recalls:** Vacant legislative seats are usually refilled in a special vote the governor calls. The lieutenant governor steps in as governor when that office is vacant, and the governor appoints replacements for other executive posts and for the state's appellate courts.
- **Administration and costs:** Counties run most elections. The Secretary of State handles statewide oversight and publishes the state voter guide. The Department of Finance estimates recall costs. The Legislature may fund the election, and leftover costs fall to the Secretary of State and counties.

**Proposal**
- **Scope:** The ballot title refers to statewide officers, but the analysis applies the changes to legislative seats too.
- **Second question removed:** "Proposition 5 removes the second question," so voters would decide only whether to remove an official.
- **Vacancy rules by office:**
  - **General rule:** Outside the governor's post, the existing vacancy process still applies.
  - **Recalled office:** "If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant."
  - **Senate and Assembly:** "a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election."
  - **Other offices:** "The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office," which includes the lieutenant governor's post.

**Governor and lieutenant governor**
- **Early-term recall** (first half of the term, before candidate filing closes ahead of the next statewide vote): "the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor."
- **Later-term recall** (outside that window): "the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term."
- **If the lieutenant governor is recalled:** The governor would pick the replacement under the "any other office" rule.
- **Not addressed:** Who would fill the lieutenant governor's own office after that person moves up to governor.

**Can recalled officials be candidates?**
Not addressed. The analysis doesn't say whether a recalled official could run to fill the vacancy.

**Fiscal effect**
- **Net effect:** Unknown. The analysis says it could be "savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars," which is "less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent)" of the General Fund.
- **What drives it:** How often recalls happen and which offices are recalled.
- **Possible costs:** The measure "could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections" if a standalone special election is needed to fill a vacancy. Each could cost millions.
- **Possible savings:** The measure "could result in lower costs" by dropping replacement-candidate information from ballots and voting materials. Savings would come from late-term governor recalls and from appointed offices.
- **Geographic reach:** A statewide recall would involve all 58 counties. A district recall would involve only that district.
- **Who pays:** Future legislative decisions would determine how costs are split between state and county governments.

- Scope: state offices only. "It does not change city or county recall procedures."

- Many executive posts would be filled by the governor's appointees. Legislative seats would typically be filled by special election, which the recalled member could enter. Judicial vacancies vary by court and county.

**Governor and Lieutenant Governor**
- Default: the Lieutenant Governor "becomes Governor for the balance of the term."
- Exception: an early-term recall qualifies only if "the recall must occur before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election," falling within the opening two years of the term. A special vote is then folded into the statewide primary. If no one wins a majority there, the two leading candidates face off in the general, and the winner finishes the term.
- Caution: "the amendment does not promise a special election after every recall in the first two years."
- Recall duties also shift. If the Governor faces a recall, the Lieutenant Governor takes on that recall work. The Controller does the same for the Secretary of State, and handles both if both are targeted.

**Can recalled officials run?**
- Not to the same seat: the text "bars the recalled official from being appointed back into the office."
- They could still seek the seat in a special election down the line, since the text "deletes the current bar on that person running in a subsequent special election."
- Judicial posts covered by Article VI, Section 16(d) keep their no-candidacy rule. The broader candidacy bar is dropped for everything else.

**Yes.** SPUR recommends voting yes on Prop. 5. Its central argument is that the measure would help California "avoid scenarios in which a successor can take statewide office with only a small plurality of votes."

**Replacement question**
- Prop. 5 would drop the same-ballot successor election and fill vacancies under existing succession rules. Governors would appoint replacements for non-legislative posts, and legislative seats would go to special elections.
- SPUR favors replacing a plurality-based special election with an institutional process tied to majority-elected officials. It calls this "a more democratic and coherent outcome than the status quo."

**Plurality problem and partisan incentives**
- Under current rules, a successor can win by finishing first, even below 50%. SPUR cites the 2003 recall, when Arnold Schwarzenegger "replaced Governor Gray Davis with only 48.6% of the vote."
- SPUR says the current setup has made recalls "an attractive strategic partisan tool for removing elected officials without majority support." It also says Prop. 5 would discourage using recalls as a shortcut around regular elections.
- SPUR notes the current system tends to favor the party out of power. Democrats have held majorities in the legislature and governor's office since 2011, so Republicans would be the likely near-term beneficiaries.

**Governor and lieutenant governor**
- Rule: "Prop. 5 would require the lieutenant governor to assume the governorship for the remainder of the term."
- A recall before nominations close for the upcoming statewide contest would trigger a special election at the following statewide primary.
- SPUR's explanation: "This special election would prevent an unelected appointed governor from holding office for a full four-year term."
- Because the lieutenant governor is elected statewide, SPUR argues succession follows established rules "rather than through a compressed, high-stakes special election."

**Recalled official's candidacy**
- Prop. 5 "removes the prohibition on recalled officers running for the same office," so a recalled official could run again for the seat in a later special election. Under current rules, the recalled official is shut out of the successor race.
- SPUR's page does not separately weigh this change.

**Special election costs**
- For legislative seats, Prop. 5 would add a separate election. SPUR warns this "could increase the cost of filling a vacancy in those seats," but the page gives no dollar estimates.

**Equity and other reasons**
- SPUR calls the equity effects mostly procedural, but argues that pluralities can "dilute the influence of any single bloc of voters, including communities of color."
- It says off-cycle elections make the electorate smaller and more lopsided. Prop. 5 would make on-cycle successor races more likely, which SPUR says reduces the risk of underrepresentation.
- Voters would face a simpler decision, and fewer might skip a recall out of concern over who would replace the official.

**Caveats**
- Lame-duck risk: SPUR's con is that the measure could "allow appointees who were not elected to hold the governorship and preside over a lame-duck period," which might make it harder to pass strong policy.
- The wording is loose. The page calls the successor an "unelected appointed governor," even though the lieutenant governor is elected statewide, so the scope of the lame-duck concern is not fully explained.
- Less direct voter input: SPUR concedes the change removes "one direct opportunity for voters to weigh in on a successor," but says the succession process "preserves a democratically legitimate alternative."

**Bottom line:** SPUR's case rests on ending plurality wins for successors and weakening partisan incentives. It acknowledges added legislative election costs, lame-duck risk, and less direct voter say on successors.

content.content:
**Source:** KQED's Prop Fest explainer, dated Sept. 30, 2026 (reporter Guy Marzorati).

**What the measure does**
- A statewide recall ballot currently asks two things: whether to remove the official, and who should take over if they're removed. Prop 5 would drop the second question, leaving only the removal question, as local recalls already do.
- It covers statewide officials (governor, attorney general, and similar offices) and state legislators in the Assembly and Senate.
- Key sentence (Marzorati): "And what proposition five would do is eliminate that second question, that question about the successor."
- Supporters call the current setup a "loophole," because the leading replacement contender can take office without a majority. Their framing: "This is a workaround where someone could potentially become governor of California without ever getting a majority vote."
- Example cited: in 2021, Republican Larry Elder won about 48% on the successor question and would have taken over from Gov. Gavin Newsom had the recall succeeded.

**Vacancy rules by office and timing**
- **Governor:** The lieutenant governor takes over.
  - *Early in the term:* A special election would be held alongside the next statewide vote, so voters pick the replacement. "there would be a special election taking place at the next statewide election"
  - *Late in the term:* The lieutenant governor serves until the next regular gubernatorial election, rather than a special election. "the lieutenant governor would simply just fill the seat until the regularly scheduled election for governor."
  - The explainer doesn't define "early" or "late."
- **Other statewide offices** (e.g., attorney general, secretary of state): The vacancy is filled by appointment. "a new attorney general will be appointed." The explainer doesn't say who appoints or how long the appointee serves.
- **State legislators:** A special election may follow removal to choose a successor. "there could be a special election called after the fact"

**Governor and lieutenant governor**
- Main objection from opponents: "the lieutenant governor would then serve as governor without ever having been elected."
- Opponents also note that the governor and lieutenant governor have almost always been Democrats, so a recall could simply install another Democrat rather than the change recall backers want.

**Can a recalled official run?** Not addressed.

**Fiscal estimate:** Not included.

**Poll**
- **Source:** Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC).
- **Date:** Released in mid-September 2026 (exact day not given; the explainer is dated Sept. 30, 2026).
- **Result:** 35% support, 59% opposed. "showed just 35% of voters supporting Proposition five with 59% opposed."
- **Not reported:** Sample size, margin of error, or question wording.

**Supporters**
- The California Democratic Party backs the measure. Nearly all of the Legislature's votes to place it on the ballot came from Democrats.
- Secretary of State Shirley Weber, the state's elections chief, is one of its leading backers: "This was a way in which people could game the system, looking for a time when we had low voter turnout."
- Proponents want the debate to focus on whether the official should be removed, not on a parallel contest over the replacement.

**Opponents**
- California's Republican Party and Republican legislators.
- Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican, leads a campaign that includes opposing the measure: "Please don't weaken the recall provision in the state constitution." "It's one of the only things we have to hold politicians accountable."
- Opponents' core argument, per the explainer: "the recall system is working as it is."

**Newsom's position:** No stated position is reported. He appears only as the target of the 2021 recall.

**Campaign money:** The reporter had not seen spending for or against the measure. "we haven't seen any campaign spending with Proposition 5 on either side."

**Recommendation:** None. The explainer lays out both sides and the poll without saying how to vote.

content.text:
**No.** It's a close call. The problem it fixes is real, but the fix is broad, permanent, and has design problems.

**Why I'd vote no**
- **It removes voters' direct say on who replaces a recalled official in several cases.** For statewide offices other than governor, the governor appoints a replacement until the next regular election. If a governor is recalled late in the term, the lieutenant governor finishes the term without a vote ([CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-proposition-explainer/)).
- **The problem is real but rare, and a narrower fix exists.** Schwarzenegger won the 2003 replacement vote with 48.6%. [SPUR](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-5-recall-process-reform) cites this. The [Sherafy guide](https://sherafy.com/california-proposition-5-2026/) notes that a runoff could fix plurality winners while keeping a direct vote on the successor.
- **Design problems.** The measure lets a recalled official run again for the seat. The [SF Chronicle](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php) calls that clause needless, and its headline says even the author doesn't like it. Legislative seats would sit vacant until a separate special election, which costs money. The [official guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/) says the net fiscal effect is unknown.
- **It's permanent and partisan in origin.** It grew out of the 2021 recall attempt against Gov. Newsom and was written by Josh Newman, who was himself recalled in 2018. Democrats placed it on the ballot largely on party lines, and the California GOP opposes it. Changing it later requires another statewide vote ([Hoover](https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-5)).
- **Newspapers and polls lean no.** Of the newspaper positions [CalMatters lists](https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), four oppose (SF Chronicle, OC Register, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News) and one supports (Sacramento Bee). Per CalMatters, PPIC had 35% yes / 59% no in September and 45% / 52% in mid-October.

**Strongest case for yes:** majority rule. Under current law, a replacement can take a governor's seat with less than half the vote. Prop 5 would route successors through majority-rule elections or ordinary appointments. SPUR, the Sacramento Bee, the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and Secretary of State Shirley Weber support it. If you think that matters more than keeping a direct vote on the replacement, vote yes.

**What I couldn't verify:** I couldn't open the measure's full text, the LAO's PDF, or PPIC's own report, so the details come from the official guide and explainers that quote the text. One CalMatters Election Day piece says Newsom endorsed Prop 5, but the other guides list no position, so I couldn't confirm it.
